title: This too is for good (Taanit 21a)
hook: Nachum of Gamzu met every setback by saying this too is for good

segments.voice: Yesterday an old man planted a carob tree for his grandchildren. Your line was plant for others. Did you start something for someone after you? Day two hundred seventy-nine.

You miss the train. The coffee spills. The email you were waiting for says no. There's a split second before you react where you get to decide what this is. A disaster? An annoyance? A story you'll tell later? One sage in the Talmud was famous for filling that split second with the same three Hebrew words, every single time. Gam zu l'tovah. This too is for good. People called him Nachum Ish Gam Zu. Nachum, the this-too man. Today, his story, and what those words do and don't mean.
screen: `THE TRAIN, THE COFFEE, THE NO.` → `A SPLIT SECOND TO DECIDE.` → `NACHUM, THE THIS-TOO MAN.`

segments.voice: Tractate Taanit tells this. The Jewish community wanted to send a gift to the emperor in Rome, and chose Nachum to carry it, because miracles seemed to follow him. They gave him a chest full of jewels. On the way he stopped at an inn. In the night, the innkeepers opened the chest, stole the jewels, and filled it with dirt. In the morning Nachum saw what had happened. And he said: this too is for good. He arrived at the palace and opened the chest before the emperor. Dirt. The emperor was furious and ordered him killed. Then the story turns. A stranger appeared among the emperor's advisers; the Talmud says it was the prophet Elijah. He said: maybe this is the dirt of their ancestor Abraham, who threw dust that turned into swords. The Romans tried it in a battle they were losing, and it worked. Nachum went home honored, his chest full of treasure. Now, a careful point. The same passage says Nachum lived with great suffering: he was blind, with no hands or feet, and his body was covered in sores. So his three words weren't a smile pasted over pain. They were a way of trusting that the story isn't finished yet. Nachum doesn't say this is good. He says this, too, is for good. The word for is doing a lot of work.
screen: `A CHEST OF JEWELS FOR ROME.` · `STOLEN, FILLED WITH DIRT.` · `THE DIRT BECOMES A WEAPON.` · `NOT GOOD: FOR GOOD.` · then, large: `GAM ZU L'TOVAH.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: try the three words on a small thing. Settle, and breathe. Pick one annoyance from this week. Not a tragedy; something small. The delayed package. The canceled plan. Picture it clearly, and notice the story you told yourself about it. Now try Nachum's words: gam zu l'tovah, this too is for good. You don't have to know how. Just leave the ending open. Notice if anything loosens. The bell holds the time.
Gam zu l'tovah. Hebrew for this too is for good. Nachum of Gamzu said it at every setback, trusting the story wasn't over.
Your line: this too for the good. Today, when one small thing goes wrong, say the three words and leave the ending open. Day two hundred seventy-nine.

screen: `DAY 279 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: IT IS NOT IN HEAVEN.`

howItsDone: Gam zu l'tovah is an everyday Jewish expression, said when plans fall through; a related saying in the Talmud, attributed to Rabbi Akiva, is that everything the Merciful One does is for good.

fork.setup: you open the emperor's gift chest and find dirt instead of jewels. what do you say?
fork.reveal: Nachum said gam zu l'tovah, and in the story the dirt turned into the emperor's victory.

original.note: Hebrew: this too is for good.

trapdoor: what it means: this too is for good; trust that the ending isn't written yet.
what a scholar hears: Gamzu is also a town in the Bible (Gimzo, 2 Chronicles 28:18), and the Talmud plays on his name.

notes: Taanit 21a paraphrased; a parallel appears in Sanhedrin 108b–109a. Abraham's dust turning to swords is a midrashic reading of Isaiah 41:2.
Whether 'Ish Gam Zu' refers to the town of Gimzo or to his saying: the Talmud gives the saying as the reason; many scholars link it to the town. Stated in the trapdoor.
Rabbi Akiva's 'all that the Merciful One does is for good' (Berakhot 60b) is a separate saying; tradition makes Akiva Nachum's student.
The suffering detail is from Taanit 21a (the house and the bed legs in water); described briefly and without drama.
